explanations.answer: Judge the living and the dead
explanations.explanation: That's exactly how Paul puts it: Christ Jesus "will judge the living and the dead" (2 Timothy 4:1). Notice he says it right as he gives Timothy a charge, so this is serious business. Paul also mentions Christ's appearing and His kingdom in the same breath. That's the kind of sentence you read standing up.

explanations.answer: Send a new prophet to Israel
explanations.explanation: I get why a big charge might sound like prophet talk, but Paul doesn't say that. He says Christ Jesus "will judge the living and the dead" (2 Timothy 4:1). Nobody is being sent anywhere in this verse. Paul is writing to Timothy, his beloved child (2 Timothy 1:2), and what he points to is Jesus as Judge.

Gathering the tribes is a big, beautiful idea, but it's not in this verse. Paul says Christ Jesus "will judge the living and the dead," and he mentions His appearing and His kingdom (2 Timothy 4:1). So the charge to Timothy comes with Jesus as Judge in view. Good guess, friend, wrong verse.

Yes, friend! Paul's list is "reprove, rebuke, and encourage" (2 Timothy 4:2). Encouragement sits right there next to the tough stuff. I think that's a good reminder that correcting and cheering somebody on can come from the same teacher.

Look at the list again. Paul says "reprove, rebuke, and encourage" (2 Timothy 4:2). So encouraging is part of the job, not something left out. The text really does say all three, and I think that's a nice balance.

There it is: "every form of patient instruction" (2 Timothy 4:2). Reproving, rebuking and encouraging all get done with patience. I think patience is easy to say and hard to do, especially when I'm waiting on a batch and the oven is taking its sweet time.
Short and sweet sounds nice, but that's not the word Paul uses. He says "every form of patient instruction" (2 Timothy 4:2). Nothing in the verse says to keep it quick. Patient is the word.

Private is a fair guess, but Paul doesn't say it. The verse says "every form of patient instruction" (2 Timothy 4:2). He doesn't tell Timothy where to do it, only how: with patience. That's the word to hold onto.

explanations.answer: Gather teachers to suit their own desires
explanations.explanation: Right on. Paul says "with itching ears they will gather around themselves teachers to suit their own desires" (2 Timothy 4:3). They don't stop listening. They just pick the teachers who say what they already want to hear. That's like asking for a recipe and only accepting the one that says cookies for dinner, forever.

explanations.answer: Stop listening to any teachers at all
explanations.explanation: Close, but they're still listening. Paul says they "will gather around themselves teachers to suit their own desires" (2 Timothy 4:3). So the teachers are still there. The people are just choosing ones who fit what they want.

explanations.answer: Leave the cities and go live alone
explanations.explanation: Nobody's packing for the wilderness in this verse. Paul says they "will gather around themselves teachers to suit their own desires" (2 Timothy 4:3). Gathering is the opposite of living alone. They want a crowd, just one that says what they want.

Yes! Paul says they "will turn their ears away from the truth and turn aside to myths" (2 Timothy 4:4). Truth walks out and myths walk in. I'd call that a bad trade, like swapping a fresh batch for a picture of cookies.
Riches show up in plenty of Scripture, but not here. Paul says they "turn their ears away from the truth and turn aside to myths" (2 Timothy 4:4). The word is myths. Hang onto that one, friend.
Idols are a big topic elsewhere in the Bible, but Paul doesn't use the word here. He says they "turn their ears away from the truth and turn aside to myths" (2 Timothy 4:4). So the answer is myths.

Not quite, friend. Paul says the opposite: "endure hardship" (2 Timothy 4:5). He doesn't tell Timothy to dodge it so the preaching can go on. Timothy is told to stay in it and do the work of an evangelist.

That's right. Paul tells Timothy to "endure hardship" (2 Timothy 4:5), not steer clear of it. The same verse says to be sober in all things, do the work of an evangelist and fulfill his ministry. Hardship is part of the road, and Timothy is told to keep walking.
That's the word: "fulfill your ministry" (2 Timothy 4:5). Paul wants Timothy to see it through. It's like a batch that goes all the way from dough to box instead of getting abandoned on the counter.
Shortening it would be the easy move, but that's not what Paul says. He says "fulfill your ministry" (2 Timothy 4:5). Fulfill means carry it all the way through, not cut it down.
A pause sounds reasonable, but Paul doesn't suggest one. He says "fulfill your ministry" (2 Timothy 4:5). I think a pause would leave the work sitting there half done, and Paul wants it fulfilled.

explanations.answer: He stayed faithful all the way to the end
explanations.explanation: That's it. Paul says "I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith" (2 Timothy 4:7). Three lines, and they all say he stayed with it. Notice he doesn't brag about being perfect. He says he kept going and kept the faith.

explanations.answer: He wishes he had done much more for God
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't sound like a man with regrets here. He says "I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith" (2 Timothy 4:7). Those are words of finishing. Nothing in the verse says he wishes for more.

explanations.answer: He is ready to start his work all over
explanations.explanation: Starting over isn't what Paul is talking about. He says "I have finished the race" (2 Timothy 4:7). A finished race is one you're done running. He's looking back at a faith he kept, not planning a restart.
Not quite, friend. Paul says the Lord will award the crown "not only to me, but to all who crave His appearing" (2 Timothy 4:8). So it's not for him alone. There's room in that promise for others.

Right. Paul says the Lord will award the crown "not only to me, but to all who crave His appearing" (2 Timothy 4:8). He includes others in the promise. I'd say that's a pretty generous thing to say at the end of a letter.

Yes, that's what he says. The crown of righteousness is something "the Lord, the righteous Judge, will award to me on that day" (2 Timothy 4:8). Paul says it's laid up for him. It's a prize he's looking forward to, and he says who hands it out.

Look at the verse again. Paul says the crown is something "the Lord, the righteous Judge, will award to me on that day" (2 Timothy 4:8). So the text really does say the Lord will award it to him. That's the whole sentence.

That's the word: "all who crave His appearing" (2 Timothy 4:8). Paul's crown is for those who long for the Lord to appear. That's also why my ovens stay ready. I don't know the day, but I keep them warm.
Miracles are wonderful, but Paul doesn't say that here. He says "all who crave His appearing" (2 Timothy 4:8). What they crave is the Lord Himself showing up. So the word is appearing.
A temple is a fair thought, but it's not what Paul says. He says "all who crave His appearing" (2 Timothy 4:8). They're longing for the Lord, not a building. Appearing is the word.
